item.title: Poor planning, lack of coordination behind Dhaka’s never ending excavation
item.description:
Roads 5, 6 and 7 in Dhanmondi have been under excavation for around seven to eight months. In Mirpur, at least 15 roads around Paris Road remain in various stages of incomplete construction.
Different neighbourhoods, same story: unplanned development work, poor coordination among utility agencies and delays in project implementation are leaving Dhaka’s roads dug up for months, causing year-round hardship for residents.
Repeated excavation disrupts daily movement, undermines road durability, damages drainage infrastructure and increases the risk of accidents, raising questions about the effectiveness of urban development planning.
In Mirpur’s Paris Road area, near Benaroshi Palli, excavation work began on several roads early this year.
A visit to the area on Thursday found at least 15 roads around Paris Road in various stages of incomplete construction, with several sections left unfinished.
On some roads, the Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) has installed drainage pipes but left the surfaces unrepaired for months.
Elsewhere, the Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (Wasa) is installing water supply lines, while additional roads have been excavated for electricity and internet connections.
A similar situation prevails in parts of Dhanmondi, where residents have been facing prolonged disruption due to overlapping development projects.
Roads 5, 6 and 7 in Dhanmondi have remained under excavation for around seven to eight months.
According to local sources, the Dhaka Power Distribution Company (DPDC) first began work to upgrade electricity lines. Wasa subsequently undertook water supply-related work, followed by a DSCC road and drainage development project.
The DSCC project, titled “Development of Roads including Street Lights, Walkways and Drainage from Kolabagan Bus Stand to Dhanmondi Road 10, Baitul Aman Mosque, Magician Street and Dhanmondi Road 05 under Ward no 15 of zone 01 of Dhaka South City Corporation”, has been allocated Tk29 crore.
The project covers 1,350 metres of roads and 2,700 metres of drains and footpaths. Work began on July 6, 2026, and is scheduled for completion on March 13, 2027.
However, the city corporation's work came after other agencies had already been operating in the area. Residents said Wasa and other agencies had been working on the same roads for at least six to seven months before the DSCC project began.
This means residents could face at least a year of disruption due to the prolonged roadwork.
Despite more than four months having passed, little visible progress has been made beyond excavation, residents said.
DSCC Zone 1 Executive Engineer Saiful Islam Joy told Dhaka Tribune that 35% of the project work had been completed, with the remaining work underway.
Shahriar Zaman, a resident of Road 7, said several roads had been excavated simultaneously, while construction was progressing at a slow pace.
“We can no longer walk on the footpaths because they have been broken up. Traffic congestion has also become a regular problem on the roads,” he said.
The consequences of uncoordinated development work are also evident in Shonir Akhra, where residents have been experiencing recurring road excavation and repair work since 2024.
Rafi Kabir, a resident of the DSCC area, told Dhaka Tribune that poor coordination between the city corporation and Wasa had resulted in newly repaired roads being excavated repeatedly.
He said the problem began when Wasa first dug up a road to install water supply pipelines. However, the contractor suddenly suspended the work before completing it.
Photo: Abir Ahmmed Shupto/ Dhaka Tribune
As Eid-ul-Azha approached, the excavated section was temporarily covered with soil without proper restoration. Nearly two months after the Eid holidays, workers returned and resumed excavation, this time digging through the middle of the road.
Residents said repeated excavation had left several roads in poor and potentially hazardous condition.
They also complained that roads were often not restored to their original condition after utility work. Uneven surfaces, raised sections and incomplete repairs obstruct vehicle movement, increase the risk of accidents and raise questions about the durability of newly constructed roads.
The disruption also extends to drainage infrastructure. Residents fear that excavation work damages existing drains, while soil and construction debris obstruct water flow.
Without proper restoration and maintenance, reduced drainage capacity could worsen waterlogging, particularly during the monsoon.
Residents of Shonir Akhra have also faced prolonged hardship over the construction of a bridge on the route to Shonir Akhra Bazar.
According to locals, the previous structure had repeatedly collapsed, making it dangerous to cross. Several accidents had occurred in the past, with people and vehicles falling into the canal and leaving many injured.
Although reconstruction was undertaken in response to longstanding public demands, residents alleged that completing the work took around six to seven months. They believe it could have been completed within a month with proper planning and timely implementation.
The timing of the work also drew criticism. Residents said the bridge should have been constructed before the road was raised and water pipelines installed. Instead, Wasa's pipeline installation and road-raising work were followed by further disruption for bridge construction.
The road has recently been reopened to traffic after months of hardship. However, residents remain apprehensive that another agency may soon begin fresh excavation.
Several officials from DSCC, Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) and Wasa told Dhaka Tribune that they were trying to coordinate road development, drainage, footpath construction, water supply pipelines and sewerage works.
They acknowledged that carrying out water supply and sewerage installations separately often results in repeated excavation, increasing public inconvenience and reducing road durability.
DSCC Chief Engineer Nur Azizur Rahman told Dhaka Tribune that the corporation regularly held coordination meetings with agencies involved in urban utility services to ensure development work was completed within stipulated deadlines.
“However, these efforts are not always effective. Wasa often fails to complete its work within the scheduled time. As a result, even when we are ready, we cannot begin our work until they finish theirs,” he said.
He explained that although the agencies wanted to complete interconnected projects within a short period, the sequence of work often prevented them from doing so.
He also pointed to jurisdictional complications, as several ministries, including the Local Government Division and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, oversee different utility agencies.
“Sometimes contractors also delay the work, citing various problems and excuses,” he added.
DNCC Chief Engineer Brig Gen Syed Rakibul Hasan, PSC, said road development projects faced multiple challenges, including poor coordination, road-related complications, deliberate delays by contractors and funding constraints.
He said different agencies had separate responsibilities and funding sources, making it difficult to complete road and sewerage projects within a short period.
He also pointed to shortcomings in Dhaka's sewerage infrastructure, saying many residential buildings lacked separate septic tanks and relied on city corporation sewerage networks.
“These systems are not suitable for handling everything. As a result, they often become dysfunctional after three to four years, forcing city corporations to excavate roads again to carry out repairs,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
He added that city corporations tried to complete projects within their scheduled timelines.
Urban planning expert and Professor Adil Mohammad Khan said coordination and timely implementation were essential to reducing public suffering.
He said city corporations had long been asking different utility agencies to submit their development plans for the coming years so that work could be scheduled according to location and priority.
However, he alleged that agencies often withheld information about their future projects due to institutional interests, weak oversight and a reluctance to share authority and accountability with other organisations.
He stressed that all agencies involved in urban development should submit at least annual work plans to the respective city corporations before undertaking excavation.
“Based on these plans, the Local Government Division can determine when and where each project should be implemented and which work should precede another,” he said.
Adil Mohammad Khan said such advance planning would allow road construction, water supply, drainage and sewerage installations to be completed in a coordinated sequence, significantly reducing repeated excavation and public inconvenience.
He urged the government to introduce a mechanism to ensure accountability and coordination among all relevant agencies.
Without integrated planning, timely implementation and proper restoration of excavated roads, Dhaka residents are likely to continue paying the price of development work through prolonged disruption to their everyday lives.

item.title: A tale of two facades: The neglect behind Murapara Rajbari’s restored front
item.description:
I first visited this place some two decades ago. Last month, yearning for a heritage site closer to home, I made a return trip to Rupganj in Narayanganj, where an educational institution now occupies the sprawling, multistoried palatial building known as Murapara Rajbari.
Hardly an hour’s drive from central Dhaka, this timeless gem retains much of its 19th-century charm—intricate designs, long colonnaded walkways, wooden beams, ornate cast-iron entrance gates, ponds, open yards, and temples.
The long colonnaded walkway features traditional wooden ceiling beams painted blue, arched openings on the left overlooking the exterior, and tall, louvered blue wooden doors leading into former palace rooms that now serve as Government Murapara College offices and classrooms. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Yet one contrast remains stark: while the front façade has received a vibrant facelift, the interior courtyards and inner chambers at the back lie dilapidated, slowly decaying beneath creeping bushes that have grown almost into a jungle.
Established by Ramratan Banerjee, the founder of the Murapara zamindar family, the Rajbari features a picturesque two-storey rectangular palace with a grand west-facing frontage. A wide verandah runs along both levels, providing access to the rooms while shielding them from the harsh western sun. Its semicircular arches are fitted with cast-iron tracery and multicolored glass, casting vivid, mosaic-like shadows across the floor.
One of the iconic ornate cast-iron entrance gates of Murapara Rajbari. At the central medallion at the very top of the gate—the intertwined iron letters form a monogram featuring a prominent “B” representing the Banerjee zamindar family, who built and expanded the estate starting in 1889. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Local lore differs slightly on the palace's exact origins. One account credits Ramratan Banerjee with constructing the entire estate, while another claims he only laid the foundation, and his descendant, Protap Chandra Banerjee, built the new palace behind the old house in 1889.
Today, the palace’s long colonnaded walkway—with its blue-painted wooden ceiling beams, arched exterior openings, and tall, louvered blue wooden doors—leads into former royal chambers that now serve as the offices and classrooms of Government Murapara College.
A weathered wooden side door and moss-covered brick wall from the older, unrenovated outbuildings of Murapara Rajbari. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Look closely at the central medallion atop the iconic main cast-iron entryway, and you will spot intertwined iron letters forming a monogram with a prominent "B" for the Banerjee family. This heavy, double-leaf gate—adorned with intricate floral scrollwork and acanthus leaf motifs—is a classic example of late 19th-century colonial-era ironwork commissioned by wealthy Bengali landlords.
A moss-covered brick archway opening into a dark, water-filled subterranean channel or culvert on the grounds of Murapara Rajbari. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
While most visitors are drawn to the arches, motifs, and surface grandeur, I was equally impressed by the architectural ingenuity behind its subterranean drainage channels, which carry away excess water while keeping the palace cool during hot summers.
One of the two matching temples stand roughly 30 feet tall on the western side of the front pond of Murapara Rajbari, built around 1889 by zamindar Ramratan Banerjee alongside the main palace. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Beyond the grand main façade, the 62-bigha estate originally housed secluded service quarters, storehouses, stables, twin temples, and high-walled enclosures around the rear pond reserved for the women of the household. While the main palace is actively maintained to support the college’s daily academic activities, the secondary structures tell a different story. The twin temples still stand, though they badly need restoration, and the older outbuildings—built with classic late-19th-century Bengali masonry of thin, kiln-fired red bricks, lime-surkhi mortar, and shallow arches over heavy timber doors—are gradually being reclaimed by monsoon moss, ferns, and banyan roots.
This close-up photo highlights the ornate ground-floor colonnade and arched transom windows of Murapara Rajbari. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
As I drove back toward the bustle of Dhaka, leaving the serene heritage grounds behind, one question stayed with me: why isn't the Department of Archaeology doing more to preserve the entirety of this architectural treasure?
This close-up photo highlights the ornate ground-floor colonnade and arched transom windows of Murapara Rajbari. Photo: Dhaka Tribune

item.title: Kathin Chibar Dan Utsab begins in Rangamati
item.description:
The 50th annual Kathin Chibar Dan Utsab, one of the largest Buddhist religious festivals in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, began at Rangamati's historic Rajban Vihar on Thursday, drawing thousands of devotees from home and abroad.
The two-day festival formally began with the inauguration of the weaving house (Bain Ghar), where devotees will weave robes for Buddhist monks within 24 hours. Rajban Vihar's resident chief, Shreemad Pragyalankar Mahasthabir, and other guests inaugurated the weaving house by cutting a ribbon.
Joyati Roy, wife of Kumar Samit Roy, a member of Chakma Circle royal family, formally began the robe-weaving ritual by spinning thread on a traditional spinning wheel.
Following the inauguration, Pragyalankar Mahasthabir delivered a religious sermon. Resident monks later circumambulated the weaving house and blessed devotees participating in the robe-making ritual.
Nirupa Dewan, vice-president of Rajban Vihar Upasak-Upasika Parishad, said the festival was the largest of its kind in the three hill districts, with Buddhist communities and indigenous people waiting throughout the year to participate.
She said devotees from Rangamati and other districts had gathered to take part in the traditional 24-hour robe-making ceremony, expressing hope that the religious occasion would bring peace and well-being to the world.
Amia Khisa, general secretary of the parishad, said the ceremony followed Buddhist religious traditions and was held after the three-month rainy-season retreat, which concludes with Prabarana Purnima.
According to Buddhist tradition, Visakha, a devoted female follower of Gautama Buddha, once made a robe from cotton within a single night and offered it to the Buddha. The tradition of Kathin Chibar Dan Utsab has continued since then.
A fair has also been set up around the vihara to mark the occasion, featuring more than a thousand stalls selling locally grown fruits and vegetables, traditional cakes, handicrafts and cottage-industry products.
Programs began with the hoisting of the Buddhist flag, followed by a religious sermon at 10:00 am on Friday for the welfare of all beings. Robes were offered to images of Gautama Buddha and Banabhante.
Kathin Chibar Dan Utsab was reintroduced in the Chittagong Hill Tracts by Buddhist religious leader Sadhananda Mahasthabir, popularly known as Banabhante. The first such ceremony at Rajban Vihar was held in 1974. Since then, the annual festival has been organised there and at its affiliated monasteries across the three hill districts.

item.title: Rain disrupts life in Satkhira, farmers fear crop losses
item.description:
Unseasonal rain has disrupted normal life in Satkhira, leaving daily wage earners and farmers struggling while raising concerns over potential damage to standing Aman paddy and mustard crops.
Rain began on Thursday morning and continued until Friday, bringing daily activities to a halt in several areas. Persistent showers and overcast skies affected the livelihoods of day-labourers and van and rickshaw pullers, many of whom struggled to find work or passengers.
The rain has also raised concerns among farmers over the harvesting of mature Aman paddy and the cultivation of mustard. However, the agriculture department said it was too early to assess the extent of possible damage.
Golam Rasul, a farmer from Kalaroa, said he had been preparing to harvest his paddy when the rain began. “If water accumulates in the fields, mature paddy and mustard seedlings could be damaged. We cannot work in the fields until the rain stops,” he said.
Gopal Das, a van puller from Rajarbagan in Satkhira town, said the rain had reduced the number of passengers. “There is hardly any work. After spending the whole day in the rain looking for passengers, it is difficult to earn enough to meet household expenses,” he said.
Plabani Sarkar, agriculture officer of Satkhira Sadar upazila, said the rain had started only that morning, making an immediate damage assessment impossible. She said rainfall could continue until Sunday and that the extent of damage could only be determined at least two days after the weather improved.
Late-planted Aman paddy is yet to be harvested and could face delays. Strong winds could cause mature plants to bend, affecting grain quality and yield. Mustard seedlings planted 15-20 days ago could also suffer damage if water remains stagnant for 36 hours or longer. Farmers have been advised to dig drainage channels to remove excess water from their fields.
Zulfikar Ali Ripon, acting officer of the Satkhira Meteorological Office, said 40mm of rainfall was recorded on Thursday. Light to moderate rain continued on Friday. Temperatures could fall to around 18-19 degrees Celsius, although a significant drop is not expected.
Meanwhile, experts have warned that sudden temperature fluctuations and damp weather could increase the risk of seasonal illnesses. High humidity, reportedly exceeding 90%, may create favourable conditions for viral, bacterial and fungal infections.

item.title: Two injured in crude bomb explosion in Kushtia
item.description:
Two men were severely injured after a crude bomb was hurled near them while they were unloading a bag of scrap material at a shop in the Mozampur area of Kushtia town on Friday afternoon.
The explosion occurred around 2:15pm near the railway line.
The injured were identified as scrap seller Suman from the Kotpara area and shop owner Ruhul Amin from Jagati Palpara.
Suman brought a bag of scrap materials on a rickshaw from Custom More to Ruhul’s shop. The blast occurred immediately as the bag was unloaded, triggering panic in the area, police and witnesses said.
Locals rescued the victims and rushed them to Kushtia General Hospital. Resident Medical Officer (RMO), Dr Iqbal Hasan of the hospital, said both sustained deep leg injuries and are receiving treatment in the surgery ward.
Officer-in-Charge Zakir Hossain of Kushtia Model Police Station, said police inspected the scene and collected evidence. He added that the victims will be questioned after recovery to determine the cause of the explosion.

item.title: PM: Armed Forces symbol of independence, sovereignty and pride
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has described the Armed Forces as a symbol of Bangladesh’s independence, sovereignty, pride and valour, saying they remain a vital national institution built on courage and discipline.
In a message issued on Friday ahead of Armed Forces Day on November 21, he said the history of the Army, Navy and Air Force was closely linked to the country’s birth and their role in the 1971 Liberation War.
Recalling November 21, 1971, the prime minister said members of the three services, alongside the Mukti Bahini, paramilitary forces and patriotic citizens, launched a coordinated counter-offensive against the Pakistani occupation forces. The day is observed annually as Armed Forces Day.
Tarique extended greetings to members of the Army, Navy and Air Force, and paid tribute to those who sacrificed their lives for the country, particularly the seven Bir Shreshthas.
He said the Armed Forces continue to protect the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity while enhancing Bangladesh’s international standing through their contributions to UN peacekeeping missions.
He also praised their role in responding to natural disasters and emergencies, saying they had earned public confidence through their service.
The prime minister recalled the contributions of former president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia to the development and modernisation of the Armed Forces.
He said the present government was taking comprehensive steps to develop a modern, technology-driven and efficient force in line with international standards.
Tarique also highlighted the Armed Forces’ role during the 2024 mass uprising and wished success to all programmes marking Armed Forces Day.

20–30 homes of activities-banned Awami League leaders and activists attacked, set on fire in Narail
item.description:
At least 20 to 30 houses belonging to leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities are banned, were set on fire in attacks allegedly carried out by BNP activists in Kalia upazila of Narail. Several houses and shops were also vandalised and looted.

The incidents reportedly took place in Bendar Char village from Friday afternoon until midnight, following the killing of two BNP leaders in the upazila.

Fire service personnel who visited the scene found 20 to 30 houses on fire. As each house in the village typically has three to four rooms, the actual number of rooms damaged by the fire could be considerably higher.

Two people were killed in an attack allegedly carried out by activists of the Awami League on a BNP motorcycle procession in Kalia upazila on Wednesday. The victims were Sohel Rana, general secretary of the Kalia upazila unit of the Jatiyatabadi Samajik Sangskritik Sangstha (JASAS), and Shahinur Islam, general secretary of the municipal unit of Jatiyatabadi Krishak Dal.

According to the victims, groups of BNP activists suddenly attacked the houses of former Awami League lawmaker BM Kabirul Haque Mukti, former municipal mayor Mushfiqur Rahman and other leaders and activists of the banned party in Bendar Char on Friday afternoon.

Around 50 houses and shops in the village were allegedly vandalised and looted, and set on fire. There were also reports of attacks, vandalism and arson at the house of Krishnapada Ghosh, general secretary of the upazila Awami League, in Boro Kalia area.

The BNP, however, has denied allegations that its activists attacked or set fire to anyone's home.

Kalia upazila BNP General Secretary SM Wahiduzzaman told journalists that the allegations of attacks on houses and arson were entirely baseless. He said claims that the incidents took place in the presence of BNP leaders were imaginary.

Meanwhile, a press release issued by the district police said reports circulating on Facebook that Hindu families' homes in Bendar Char had been vandalised, looted and set on fire were false and fabricated.

The press release alleged that leaders and activists of the Awami League were publishing previously recorded and AI-generated videos on Facebook and other social media platforms to deliberately tarnish the image of the government and the country at home and abroad.

The police said there were no Hindu settlements in Bendar Char and that neither any Hindu family nor any business establishment had been attacked.

Asked about allegations of attacks on Hindu settlements, SM Wahiduzzaman said 90 per cent of members of the Hindu community in the area had voted for the BNP in the last parliamentary election. He said the BNP stood with the Hindu community and that its members also supported the party.

"I see on Facebook that more than 200 houses were attacked. This is completely false," he said.

Police statement on the attacks

According to the police press release, following the killing of the two BNP leaders, their aggrieved relatives and several other people gathered in Bendar Char village at around 4:45pm on Friday.

They attacked several houses belonging to leaders and activists of the banned Awami League who were allegedly involved in the killings before leaving the area.

On receiving the information, police from Kalia Police Station visited the scene and brought the situation under control. The situation is now normal, the press release said, adding that additional police personnel had been deployed in the area.

Narail Superintendent of Police Mohammad Al Mamun Sikder told Prothom Alo over the phone on Saturday afternoon that relatives and supporters of the two slain BNP leaders had vandalised three to four houses in the village.

He said the area was not predominantly Hindu and that the incident was not as it was being portrayed.

Fire service account of the arson

Humayun Kabir, station officer of the Kalia upazila fire service, told journalists that the fire broke out around 4pm on Friday.

Nobody called the fire service. They could not reach the area immediately because of obstructions and security concerns, he said.

They eventually reached the scene around 8pm. By then, fires had broken out at many houses, although their intensity was relatively low.

Firefighters extinguished some of the fires, while others went out on their own, he said.

Kabir estimated that 20 to 30 houses had caught fire. As each house typically has three to four rooms, the number of rooms affected could be considerably higher..

item.title: FCPS Part 1 exams begin 1 Dec, routine published
item.description:
The routine for the written examination of the January 2027 session of FCPS Part-I has been published.

According to the routine released by the Bangladesh College of Physicians and Surgeons (BCPS), the examination will begin on 1 December and continue until 3 December.

The four-hour examination will be held from 9:00am to 1:00pm each day at the BCPS building in Mohakhali, Dhaka.

A total of 65 subjects will be covered in this year's examination under the fellowship programme. Of these, 27 are general subjects and 38 are specialised subjects.

The examinations in Medicine and Allied, Biochemistry, Community Medicine, Family Medicine, Haematology, Microbiology, Pathology, and Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation will be held on 1 December.

On 2 December, examinations will be held in Anaesthesiology, Anatomy, Dermatology and Venereology, Forensic Medicine, Ophthalmology and Allied, Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery, Pharmacology, Physiology, Psychiatry and Allied, Radiology and Imaging, Radiotherapy, Surgery and Allied, and Transfusion Medicine.

On 3 December 2026, examinations will be held in Dental Surgery (Conservative Dentistry and Endodontics, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopaedics, and Prosthodontics), Obstetrics and Gynaecology and Allied, and Paediatrics and Allied.

item.title: FBI, USAD breached by hackers: reports
item.description:
The US Agriculture Department and the FBI were breached by hackers in cyberattacks, US media reported on Friday, as concerns deepened over the recent spate of tech outages at key American institutions.

Major outages in recent weeks have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users across the United States, even affecting a top-secret network at the National Security Agency.

US President Donald Trump has sought to calm the public and urged people to "relax", while officials said the various outages were not linked to criminal activity.

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyberattack, NBC reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials.

The hackers may use the payments system as a backdoor to access more sensitive material, the former officials told NBC.

The USDA deals with "a bunch of scary biologic issues" and "if an adversary or a competitor were to have access to that same information... they could use our own research against us," a former official was quoted as saying.

CNN said separately on Friday that the FBI was hacked for the second time since September.

The federal agency was investigating an intrusion of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) by apparent hackers, CNN reported citing two people briefed on the probe.

The NCIC has a nationwide criminal information database linking federal, state and local law enforcement and is used to share information on warrants and background checks.

"Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety," a former FBI official told CNN.

The former official expressed concerns that hackers "could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on."

AFP has contacted the FBI and USDA for comment.

The newly uncovered breaches at the FBI and USDA were described as hacks, which are different from outages like the ones that afflicted Microsoft Outlook and the Federal Aviation Administration.

In September, a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.

The White House fired cybersecurity chief Sean Cairncross this week as criticism mounted over the string of major outages.

item.title: Who will implement the verdict on the Rohingya?
item.description:
The 19 November verdict delivered by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on the Rohingya of Myanmar immediately made headlines in media outlets around the world. Reached after several years of legal battles, the verdict is significant in many ways and for many parties. However, the process for its legal implementation remains unclear.

The ICJ’s ruling that Myanmar is responsible for the genocide of the Rohingya represents a major moral victory for the community. It is likely to increase global sympathy for them. The verdict has reaffirmed that the Rohingya were not in a good situation in Myanmar and that the remaining members of the community there continue to face threats.

The language of the verdict will also serve as a significant affirmation of the Rohingya’s rights as citizens of Myanmar. It has further strengthened their demand to return to their homeland. Moreover, the global attention and sympathy generated by the ruling could lead to increased aid and assistance for refugee camps. It may also reduce efforts to deport Rohingya refugees who have sought shelter in various countries around the world. On the contrary, countries may become more willing to offer them refuge.

The ICJ verdict has also strengthened Bangladesh’s position on the Rohingya issue. The ruling provides strong justification for Bangladesh’s decision to shelter a community facing genocide. It could also lead to increased international assistance for their upkeep in the future, which would come as a relief to Bangladesh.

More importantly, the verdict has undoubtedly strengthened Bangladesh’s bargaining position in negotiations with Myanmar over the repatriation of the Rohingya. Another reality that has emerged in the aftermath of the ruling is that Bangladesh cannot, under any circumstances, forcibly send the Rohingya back to Rakhine state. The government in Dhaka, of course, has never wanted to do so.

Following this verdict, all eyes will be on Myanmar’s government and armed forces. The prospects for the Rohingya’s return and rehabilitation will depend on how they respond to the ruling in the long run. So far, they appear to be dismissing it. In an immediate reaction posted on its Telegram channel, a spokesperson for the Myanmar government said there was “nothing to worry about” regarding the verdict.

However, the ruling is undoubtedly a diplomatic blow to General Min Aung Hlaing. It remains to be seen whether China will continue to invite a junta of this kind for visits or extend cooperation to it as comfortably as before. Moreover, Indonesia and Malaysia are likely to raise questions about the representation of General Min’s government at ASEAN meetings. Both countries are considered sympathetic to the Rohingya cause. Trade and commercial dealings with a government accused of genocide could also become problematic for many countries.

Overall, ASEAN will have to reconsider its long-standing indifference towards the Rohingya crisis. Continuing to accommodate General Min Aung Hlaing at the bloc’s meetings could become an increasingly sensitive issue for the organisation.

Arakan Army has long controlled much of northern Arakan, a region historically inhabited by a large Rohingya population. Yesterday’s verdict will also compel the Arakan Army to reconsider its position on the Rohingya question

The verdict is also encouraging for pro-democracy forces in Myanmar. Although the genocide against the Rohingya took place during Aung San Suu Kyi’s tenure, those opposing the military junta have already changed their position on this persecuted community. They have pledged to recognise the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group. Moreover, the military, which has deprived the country of democracy, has now been identified as a perpetrator of genocide. This has further strengthened the legitimacy of the human rights activists’ struggle in the country.

Understandably, the ICJ verdict has also stirred things up across Rakhine State. Although the ruling has renewed the significance of the Rohingya’s demand to return to the region, the central armed forces, known as the Tatmadaw, now control only a small part of the state. The Arakan Army has long controlled much of northern Arakan, a region historically inhabited by a large Rohingya population. Yesterday’s verdict will also compel the Arakan Army to reconsider its position on the Rohingya question.

Rohingyas must be repatriated to Myanmar as per verdict: Foreign Minister

The Myanmar government does not recognise the Rohingya as citizens of the country or as a distinct ethnic group. The Arakan Army recognises them as citizens, but not as a distinct ethnic group; instead, it regards them as ‘Bengalis’.

The International Court’s emphasis and directives on the rehabilitation of the Rohingya have also put pressure on the Arakan Army to review its position on the issue. In particular, if it hopes to secure international support for its own ethnic struggle, the Arakan Army now has a moral responsibility to cooperate in the rehabilitation of the Rohingya.

The key question following the verdict is undoubtedly: what practical significance will it have? Who will bring the perpetrators of genocide to justice? For now, there is no clear answer to this question. Another question has also resurfaced: will the international community take any new initiatives to facilitate the Rohingya’s return to Rakhine State?

Given the current realities, even if both the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army agree to the Rohingya’s return, it will be necessary to establish a safe zone in parts of Rakhine State. Without such a zone, the Rohingya will not be able to live there in security and comfort over the long term. However, if such a zone is established, an international presence will be needed to oversee it.

In this regard, Bangladesh could certainly be called upon to play an important role. However, a major question remains: will China agree to the establishment of such a potential safe zone inside Rakhine State? China considers Myanmar part of its security sphere and has substantial strategic investments in Rakhine, also known as Arakan. Any international presence in the region would therefore have to take China’s views into account. Moreover, neither the Arakan Army nor the Tatmadaw would agree to such an initiative without China’s tacit approval.

Doing business with the junta, helps to sustain atrocities in Myanmar

Recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group and the restoration of their citizenship rights are also essential for their repatriation. Persuading the Tatmadaw and the Arakan Army to agree to these demands will only be possible if China takes a sympathetic position on the issue. Following this verdict, China’s role has once again emerged as an indirectly crucial factor.

However, the verdict has already placed China’s longstanding and unwavering support for Myanmar’s military under moral scrutiny. Unless China takes a constructive position on implementing the ruling, it will face increasingly difficult questions in the international arena in the future.

* Altaf Parvez is a writer and researcher.

item.title: Met on dating app, held hostage for 4 days, loses nearly Tk 8 lakh
item.description:
After connecting with someone through a dating app, Tawhid Hossain (pseudonym) went to meet the person in front of Shaheed Police Smriti College in Dhaka. Upon meeting, the individual took him to a nearby apartment. As soon as he entered, several people who had been waiting inside restrained him and beat him up. They then began demanding money.

Tawhid was rescued by the Mirpur division of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police's Detective Branch (DB) in an operation on 13 November afternoon. According to the DB, the gang held him captive for four days and extorted nearly Tk 8 lakh from him in several instalments. A case has been filed at Kafrul Police Station in connection with the incident.

Police and other sources said Tawhid is a freelancer who earns Tk 1.5 lakh to Tk 2 lakh a month. He lives with his wife and child. He has accounts on several dating apps but claims he had never previously contacted anyone through those platforms. He said he fell victim to a scam when he went to meet someone he had met online for the first time.

DB sources said, Tawhid had accounts on two social networking and dating apps, one called ‘QK’ and the other ‘HeeSay’. The apps allow users to view profiles and photographs of people in nearby areas and contact them based on their preferences. The QK app also offers private messaging, voice chat and live streaming.

DB sources said investigators uncovered a fraud syndicate while investigating the incident. The gang had been using dating apps to lure people into traps and extort money for a long time. The members call the practice ‘catching chickens’ in their jargon. Police are conducting operations to arrest the other members of the gang.

Lured into a trap, money transferred in instalments

According to DB, Tawhid met a man named Rocky through an app on 8 November. Rocky invited him to meet the following day at around 10:30am. After meeting in front of Shaheed Police Smriti College, Rocky suggested going to a nearby house.

Once there, Rocky, Rony, Asif and several others restrained Tawhid. Another five to six people were already inside the house. Police have yet to identify them.

Investigators said Tawhid was beaten while being held at the house. The gang members then checked the bKash, Nagad and banking apps on his mobile phone to determine how much money he had.

As a freelancer, Tawhid had money deposited in several bank accounts. Although none of the accounts contained a large sum individually, each held around Tk 40,000 to Tk 50,000.

Investigators said the gang members took his phone after beating him and forced him to disclose the PINs needed to access his bank accounts through mobile banking apps. Tawhid gave them the PINs after pleading with them not to inform his family.

The scammers subsequently transferred money from his bank accounts to various bKash accounts. They withdrew the money in small amounts through different agents before collecting it in cash.

After taking all the money from Tawhid, the gang contacted his wife and demanded ransom from her as well.

DB said Tawhid's wife contacted law enforcement after receiving the call. Using information technology, detectives tracked down the location and rescued Tawhid on 13 November afternoon.

The gang had extorted nearly Tk 8 lakh from him over the four days he was held captive. Police have recovered Tk 1.8 lakh of the money so far and are working to recover the rest.

Acquainted while using drugs, later joined the scam

According to DB, three members of the gang were arrested during the operation. They are Md Asif (2), Md Ali (21) and Ronok Hossain (18).

Md Ali and Ronok were arrested at the house, while Asif was detained elsewhere. However, the alleged masterminds, Rocky and Rony, remain at large. Police are conducting operations to arrest them.

Citing interrogation findings, the DB said Asif had become involved in this type of fraud for the first time. He was unemployed and lived in Savar. He came to Dhaka on 1 November in search of work.

On 3 November, he met Rony through another person while using drugs. He later joined the gang at Rony's invitation, hoping to earn more money.

The gang used the same tactics in other scams

DB officials said gang members opened multiple fake accounts on different apps to hide their identities and contact people. They would then invite their targets to meet at a designated location, where they would detain them and extort money.

The gang has both male and female members, whom it deploys depending on the circumstances.

Investigators said the gang had previously carried out four similar incidents, extorting several lakh taka from victims. Preliminary findings suggest it had extorted around Tk 20 lakh in total. Police are also trying to contact the other victims.

‘Scammers are exploiting the growing use of dating apps’

Mohammad Rakib Khan, deputy commissioner of the DB's Mirpur division, told Prothom Alo that scam gangs are exploiting the growing tendency to use dating apps.

People attracted to the same sex are increasingly using these apps, he said. Many victims are reluctant to disclose such incidents because of social stigma, allowing the gangs to exploit their vulnerability.

Mohammad Rakib Khan further said the gang's masterminds were not present at the house during the operation. Police are conducting operations to arrest them and recover the remaining money.

Investigators are also examining the mobile phones of the arrested suspects and questioning them to gather information about previous incidents.

item.title: 90 BGB platoons deployed in 8 districts, including Dhaka, Gopalganj; drones, body-worn cameras to be used
item.description:
A total of 90 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in Dhaka and seven other districts to maintain law and order, ensure public security and prevent any untoward incidents.

According to a BGB press release issued today, Saturday the deployment covers Dhaka, Narayanganj, Gazipur, Gopalganj, Mymensingh, Faridpur and Cox's Bazar districts.

Of the deployed forces, 18 platoons have been deployed in Dhaka district, five in Dhaka metropolitan city, six in Narayanganj, 15 in Gazipur, 29 in Gopalganj, two in Mymensingh, five in Faridpur and six in Cox's Bazar.

Another four platoons have been kept on standby for deployment if necessary.

The BGB personnel will perform their duties in coordination with the respective district administrations and other law enforcement agencies in line with instructions from the Ministry of Home Affairs.

They will strengthen security and surveillance at key installations, industrial zones and other important locations while taking measures to prevent disorder, violence and activities that could threaten public safety.

Meanwhile, technology-based surveillance is being maintained through a monitoring cell at BGB Headquarters to closely observe the ground situation and ensure effective coordination.

Live footage from drones, body-worn cameras and other modern surveillance equipment is being monitored round the clock, the release said.

The BGB personnel are carrying out their assigned duties alongside their regular border responsibilities, maintaining professionalism, discipline and patience.

The force remains committed to protecting people's lives and property, facilitating normal movement and daily activities, and taking necessary precautionary measures to deal with any untoward situation, it added.

item.title: 7,000 medical technologists, pharmacists to be recruited; circular likely in December
item.description:
The government is planning to recruit around 7,000 medical technologists and pharmacists to strengthen the country's healthcare services. Of the proposed recruitment, around 5,000 posts are expected to be for medical technologists and nearly 2,000 for pharmacists.

The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has sought updated information from health facilities across the country to determine the exact number of vacant posts.

A notice regarding the major recruitment for around 10,000 posts, including the 5,000 medical technologists and 2,000 pharmacists, is expected to be issued by mid-December this year.

"We have requested information from every health facility instead of relying solely on Management Information System (MIS) data. After receiving and compiling the information, we will finalise the recruitment requirements," DGHS Additional Director General (ADG) Prof Dr Jalal Uddin Mohammad Rumi told BSS.

He said the DGHS is also preparing to recruit around 150 employees in different categories, including accounts assistants, accountants and office assistants. The recruitment notice for this process is expected within the next two weeks.

The ADG said recruitment of health assistants was also underway at the district level, with the process completed in some areas and ongoing in others. However, recruitment in certain districts has been delayed due to pending court cases, he added.

Explaining measures to ensure transparency in government recruitment, Prof Rumi said appointments to non-medical posts under grades 11 to 20 would be conducted through designated recruitment committees comprising officials from the DGHS, the Public Service Commission (PSC), the Ministry of Public Administration or the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Health.

The Director (Administration) of the DGHS serves as the committee chairman, while the Deputy Director (Administration) acts as its member secretary, he said.

The recruitment committee will determine the examination policy, followed by written tests and viva examinations. The written examination will maintain standards followed by the PSC, the ADG added.

He said the written examination process would be conducted under the recruitment committee's supervision, with answer scripts evaluated before the results are announced, as part of efforts to ensure transparency.

Prof Rumi also clarified that recruitment of doctors under the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) cadre, including graduate medical and dental doctors, is conducted through the PSC. Some other non-medical posts under grades 7 and 9 are also filled through the commission.

Regarding allegations of corruption in the health sector, he said immediate administrative measures could include placing officials suspected of misconduct on Officer on Special Duty (OSD) status or removing them from their positions.

The ADG, however, said that, to his knowledge, no departmental case has so far been initiated specifically over corruption-related allegations. Most departmental proceedings initiated so far concerned absenteeism and misconduct, he added.

On ensuring the proper use of medical equipment, he said the DGHS has issued strict instructions to field-level health facilities to ensure the effective utilisation and timely repair of equipment lying unused or out of order.

He said concerned authorities have been instructed to dispose of official correspondence swiftly.

Besides, initiatives are underway to make divisional-level offices more functional alongside the central Transport and Equipment Maintenance Organization (TEMO), Prof Rumi said, adding that a Development Project Proposal (DPP) is being prepared to this end.

item.title: Alves now a preacher: Leaving behind multi-million life, he seeks happiness on 113 euro
item.description:
That was all Dani Alves earned from working inside prison. Once a dominant figure on the pitch for Barcelona and Brazil, he earned millions upon millions of euros during his football career. Now, however, he stands before thousands of people and says he was happier earning those 113 euro in prison.

The statement may sound simple. But a closer look reveals two very different lives standing side by side. On one side are the glittering nights at Camp Nou and the applause of thousands of spectators. On the other are the silent corridors of a prison, where a person is left to confront himself more than ever.

Alves recently made these remarks while recalling the 14 months he spent at Brians 2 Prison near Barcelona. He is now a preacher. Speaking at a religious gathering, he said, “I used to earn millions of euros, thank God. But I was happier earning 113 euro in prison than I was when I earned millions of euros!” What did he find in those 113 euro that millions of euros could not give him?

To understand the Alves of today, it is worth looking back. He once dominated the right flank on the football pitch, surging forward in attack and tracking back whenever his team needed him in defence. The entire football world became familiar with his tireless runs during Barcelona's golden era.

According to Barcelona's statistics, Alves won 46 trophies during his career. He scored 23 goals in 409 appearances for the Catalan club and won 23 trophies with them, including three Champions League titles and six La Liga titles. He also won Serie A with Juventus and the French league title twice with Paris Saint-Germain (PSG).

Alves made 126 appearances for Brazil. He won the Copa América in 2007 and 2019, as well as the FIFA Confederations Cup in 2009 and 2013. His trophy collection is enviable, and his list of achievements is extensive. Yet, despite all this success, Alves now believes that achievement and happiness do not always go hand in hand.

Dani Alves, former Brazilian footballerI was imprisoned for 40 years, but it was in prison that I found true freedom.

In December 2022, Alves faced allegations of sexually assaulting a young woman at a nightclub in Barcelona. Police arrested him in January 2023. In February 2024, a court sentenced him to four and a half years in prison. He had already spent nearly 14 months behind bars before the trial. In March that year, he secured provisional release on bail of one million euro.

In March 2025, however, Catalonia's High Court overturned the earlier verdict on appeal and acquitted him of the charges. The court found several inconsistencies in the original ruling and concluded that the evidence was insufficient to rebut the presumption of innocence. That chapter of his legal battle has ended. But, for Alves, freedom appears to carry a deeper and more personal meaning.

Recently, while reflecting on how his life had changed, Alves wrote, “I was imprisoned for 40 years, but it was in prison that I found true freedom. For 40 years, I was bound by my sins, my mistakes and my decisions. From the outside, I might have appeared free, but inside I was chained.”

He added, “I am not free simply because I have left prison. I am free because Jesus has freed me from sin. True freedom does not depend on where your feet are, but on who reigns in your heart.” Speaking about his relationship with God, his tone became even softer: “I ask Him many questions. I am like a child before Him. I ask Him about everything.”

Now 43, Alves stands on religious platforms rather than football pitches. He recently travelled to Argentina to deliver religious speeches. He is also a co-owner of Portuguese club São João de Ver. Alves has moved from the right flank of the football pitch to a very different stage in life. However, not everything in this new chapter of his life appears to be going smoothly.

Alves' wife is Spanish model Joana Sanz. The couple married in 2017 and have been together for almost nine years. Their daughter was born in October 2025. On 13 November, one of Joana's Instagram followers asked whether she accompanied her husband to religious events. In response, Joana wrote, “I do not believe in (religion). The more I see what he is doing, the more distant I feel from religion. I want to make one thing clear: we have been living separately for some time. That is precisely why.”

This was the first time news of their separation became public. According to Spanish media reports, the couple are going through divorce proceedings. Journalist Javi Hoyos reportedly said that Joana had increasingly felt lonely because Alves frequently travelled abroad for his religious preaching activities.

A man who once earned millions of euros says he found greater happiness in receiving a modest sum in prison.

An even more pointed response followed. On 15 November, Alves' religious message circulated on an Instagram account called “Ministerio de Adoración”. In the message, he said that Jesus had stood by him during the difficult times in prison, even when his friends and those closest to him had walked away.

The following day, on 16 November, Joana responded: “How dare you say publicly that only Jesus stood by you?” Joana claimed that she had visited Alves in prison, spent Christmas with him instead of with her own family, and paid his bills and debts with her own money. She further alleged that Alves had eventually pushed her away. She said she then stepped aside at his request. These are Joana's personal claims, which she has shared publicly on social media. Alves has yet to respond publicly.

Meanwhile, another financial lawsuit has come to light. On 12 November, a court in São Paulo ordered restrictions on the transfer of ownership of two of Alves' properties and a Porsche. An investment firm named GAD Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios filed the lawsuit, claiming that Alves owed it around 7 million Brazilian reais, equivalent to approximately Tk 170 million (17 crore).

The firm claims that it acquired the rights to money owed to Alves after he terminated his contract with São Paulo FC in 2021. Although the agreement required payment, the payments later stopped. The firm subsequently filed a lawsuit.

However, the court's order does not constitute a final decision to seize the properties. The case remains pending. The 7 million (70 lakh) reais represents the amount claimed by the firm, not a debt conclusively established by the court. Alves' representatives have also yet to issue an official response.

It seems as though several matches are unfolding simultaneously in one man's life. At home, he faces the turmoil of a broken marriage. In court, he faces a financial lawsuit. On social media, personal allegations and counter-allegations continue. Yet the same man stands on religious platforms and declares that he is free.

Ultimately, no one can say for certain who is right and who is wrong. There is a court ruling, Joana's allegations and Alves' personal beliefs. Even after considering all three, one statement by Alves continues to linger in the mind: “I was happier earning 113 euro!”

A man who once earned millions of euros says he found greater happiness in receiving a modest sum in prison. Perhaps, for him, that happiness meant finding freedom from remorse and surrendering himself to God.

On the football pitch, Alves knew that the further a player advances down the right flank, the longer the journey back can become. For an attacking full-back, the greatest risk lies in the space left behind. When the team loses possession, opponents exploit that gap to launch an attack.

Perhaps Alves has also travelled a long way on the field of life. But reality continues to catch up with him through the gaps left by broken relationships, old debts and unspoken words. And he continues to walk forward, carrying that burden in his own way, perhaps a little more alone.

item.title: PM pays tribute to Armed Forces martyrs
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Saturday paid tribute to the martyred members of the Bangladesh Armed Forces on the occasion of Armed Forces Day 2026.

He paid homage by placing wreaths at the altar of Shikha Anirban (flame eternal) at Dhaka Cantonment this morning, expressing deep respect for the memory of the armed forces members who made the supreme sacrifice in the 1971 Liberation War.

After laying the wreath, he stood in solemn silence for a while as a mark of profound respect for the martyrs.

A contingent of the Army, Navy and Air Force presented a guard of honour while the bugle sounded the last post.

The prime minister later signed the visitors' book kept at the memorial.

Earlier, upon his arrival at Shikha Anirban, he was received by the chiefs of the three services and senior officials of the Armed Forces Division.

Army Chief General Waker-Uz-Zaman, Navy Chief Admiral Khondkar Misbah Ul Azim and Air Chief Air Chief Marshal Hasan Mahmood Khan also jointly placed wreaths at Shikha Anirban on behalf of their respective forces.

After placing the wreath, the prime minister went to the Armed Forces Division, where the chiefs of three services paid a courtesy call on him.

Later, the premier attended a reception for selected gallantry award-winning freedom fighters and their heirs at the Army Multipurpose Complex in Dhaka Cantonment. Around 101 freedom fighters and their successors took part in the programme. After the reception, the prime minister joined the freedom fighters and their heirs at a tea session.

Special programmes were taken up at all cantonments, naval bases and installations, and air force bases across the country to mark Armed Forces Day, PM's Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony said.

The day's programmes began with special munajat at mosques after Fajr prayers, seeking the welfare and prosperity of the country, continued progress of the Armed Forces and eternal peace for the souls of the martyred members of the Armed Forces.

Earlier in the day, President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir also paid tribute at Shikha Anirban and signed the visitors' book.

On this day in 1971, the Army, Navy and Air Force launched a coordinated offensive against Pakistani occupation forces, which hastened the country's victory in the Liberation War. The day has been observed as Armed Forces Day every year since independence.

A reception will also be hosted on behalf of the prime minister at Senakunja in Dhaka Cantonment at 4 pm.

item.title: Foreign nationals from India, Myanmar, Taiwan, Pakistan, China come to Bangladesh and commit crimes
item.description:
A section of foreign nationals in Bangladesh is increasingly becoming involved in various crimes, including online fraud, gambling, narcotics, gold smuggling, and illegal infiltration. Over the past two years, law enforcement agencies have arrested 633 citizens from various countries in connection with such offences.

These foreign nationals were arrested between 5 August 2024 and September of this year. The largest contingent among them is from India, numbering 346. Charges against Indian nationals prominently include illegal infiltration, narcotics trafficking, and the smuggling of gold and other contraband.

Following India, the arrested foreigners include 62 from Myanmar, 61 from Taiwan, 35 from Laos, 24 from Pakistan, and 22 from China.

Additionally, there is one each from Vietnam and Nepal, alongside 81 nationals from several other countries, including Nigeria, Somalia, and Thailand. They face charges ranging from online fraud, fake cryptocurrency or fraudulent investment schemes, and operating scam centres to drug trafficking.

According to the Department of Prisons, 127 of the arrested foreign nationals have already been released on bail.

On 11 November, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) arrested two Indian nationals with arms and ammunition roughly 150 yards inside Bangladeshi territory in the Minatila border area of Jaintiapur upazila, Sylhet. 

Identified as Batim Tuta, 28, and Tempo, 20, they had entered Bangladesh illegally; the BGB recovered a firearm, 35 rounds of ammunition, and two machetes from their possession.

Earlier, on 27 August, the Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) detained two Indian nationals arriving at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka on a Thai Airways flight with 5.12 kg of the drug Kush. A case was filed against them at the Airport police station under the Narcotics Control Act. 

Prior to that, the DNC arrested one Indian citizen with three kg of Kush on 22 August, and two more with five kg of Kush on 24 August.

According to data from the Police’s Special Branch (SB) and law enforcement agencies, as many as 2,268,065 people from various countries entered Bangladesh over the 26 months between the student-mass uprising on 5 August 2024 and September this year. Of them, 7,088 citizens from 126 countries are residing illegally in Bangladesh after their visas expired. Indian nationals top this list at 2,164, followed by Chinese nationals at 1,995. However, not all overstaying foreigners are engaged in criminal activities.

Law enforcement records indicate that a large proportion of illegally staying foreigners work in various private companies, residing predominantly in Dhaka, Gazipur, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Pabna, Cumilla, and Narayanganj.

According to police officials, those inclined towards criminal activity generally hail from specific countries. Most arrived in Bangladesh on business or tourist visas, while some entered on visas-on-arrival and stayed on illegally. Several deliberately destroy their passports, exploiting General Diaries (GDs) filed for lost passports and protracted legal proceedings to prolong their stay in Bangladesh.

The criminal operations of these foreign nationals are diverse. Syndicates defraud victims by promising lucrative returns on gold or Bitcoin investments within a short timeframe, luring people via social media friendships with promises of expensive gifts from abroad, and dangling attractive online earning opportunities.

Law enforcement agencies also possess intelligence on foreign nationals engaging in bank ATM booth and credit card fraud, online casinos or gambling, narcotics trafficking, mobile banking scams, counterfeiting currency, illegal VoIP operations, gold smuggling, money laundering, and human trafficking.

Speaking about this, Additional Inspector General of Police (Additional IGP) at Police Headquarters, Md Ahsan Habib Palash, told Prothom Alo that foreign nationals with expired visas are engaging in crimes. Upon securing bail after arrest, many return to the same offences. In those cases, they were being brought to justice repeatedly.

On 11 September, police raided a building in the Jalalabad residential area under Khulshi police station in Chattogram city, arresting 70 foreign nationals on charges of operating an online fraud ring modelled on scam centres. Police also seized 170 electronic devices from their possession. 

Earlier, on the night of 3 September, acting on intelligence from Dhaka police tracing a complaint lodged at Ramu police station, police raided a hotel in Cox’s Bazar town and arrested six foreign nationals belonging to a similar syndicate.

Those arrested in the Chattogram and Cox’s Bazar raids include nationals from China, Pakistan, Laos, Nepal, Vietnam, and Taiwan. Police intelligence indicates they were attempting to establish scam or fraud centres inside Bangladesh.

Notably, scam centres based in Cambodia and Myanmar—where victims are trafficked under the guise of high-paying jobs and subsequently held hostage—have recently drawn global scrutiny, with many Bangladeshi citizens among the victims.

Additional IGP (Crime and Operations) Md Ahsan Habib Palash explained that a foreign syndicate had previously taken several Bangladeshis to Cambodia to set up scam centres, and is now plotting to establish similar operations inside Bangladesh with their assistance—a development law enforcement agencies are keeping under close surveillance.

Past figures also showed high numbers of illegal stays

Previous records also pointed to large numbers of foreign nationals staying illegally and engaging in crime in Bangladesh. 

According to an earlier SB data, between October 2014 and October 2023, some 726 citizens from 33 countries were accused in various criminal cases. Nigerians accounted for the highest number at 91, followed by Pakistan (28) and Cameroon (17). During that timeframe, 137 nationals from 14 countries were arrested, mostly on charges of fraud, ATM card skimming, and drug trafficking.

As of October 2023, out of 86,962 foreign nationals residing in Bangladesh, 42,429 had overstayed their visas. Among the illegal residents, 5,597 had entered on visas-on-arrival, while others arrived on business, tourist, student, or athlete visas.

Smuggling medicines via courier

On 14 October, SRB-3 (Special Response Battalion) conducted a raid in Dhaka’s Uttara and arrested four individuals, including a Chinese national, for smuggling life-saving drugs—including cancer medications—abroad via courier. Medicines worth approximately Tk 75 million and TK 600,000 in cash were seized from their possession.

SRB-3 Commanding Officer Lieutenant Colonel Fayezul Arefin stated that the syndicate bought medicines at low prices in Bangladesh, evading government duties, and smuggled them to countries including Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam. 

The arrested Chinese national, Li Fen, repeatedly entered Bangladesh on a 30-day tourist visa, departing just before expiration before returning on a fresh visa.

Embezzlement under the guise of investment

In July 2025, the then-RAB arrested two Nigerian nationals and their Bangladeshi accomplice from Bashundhara and Pallabi in Dhaka on charges of embezzling money through fraudulent investment lures on Facebook. 

According to law enforcement officials, the syndicate posed as wealthy foreigners, promising high investment returns and expensive gifts from abroad, swindling Tk 1.8 to 2 million from over 100 victims. Both arrested Nigerians had expired visas.

Similarly, on 3 August 2023, police arrested four people, including two Chinese nationals, from Satkania in Chattogram for running a fake Amazon-style website that defrauded victims by promising a monthly income of Tk 18,000 for working 20 minutes a day. 

Police uncovered the ring while investigating a case filed by a defrauded former government official.

Complications in crime control and repatriation

Law enforcement officials point out that some arrested foreign offenders resume criminal activities once released on bail, while overstaying foreigners exploit lost-passport GDs and prolonged trial timelines to remain in the country. Moreover, the financial burden of repatriating deported nationals falls on the Bangladesh government, posing an additional hurdle to deportation.

Commenting on foreign nationals involved in criminal activities, Director General of the Special Response Battalion (SRB) Faruque Ahmed told Prothom Alo that crime involving foreigners has not yet reached extreme proportions.

Operations will be launched to bring them to justice upon government directives, he added.
